newsitem.title: JAPAN: Swimming-Australian youth movement looks to 2000.
newsitem.headline: Swimming-Australian youth movement looks to 2000.

text.p: Australia's swimming machine has taken on some new blood, including a 14-year-old nicknamed "Thorpedo", as it eyes its goal of the Sydney Summer Olympics in 2000.
"It's part of the process," head Australian coach Don Talbot said at the Pan Pacific Championships. "We are identifying young people for 2000."

Talbot, who brought seven coaches with him to help oversee the 34 swimmers, including 17 teenagers, he has competing in Fukuoka, said the Australian government is spending more money to support sports programmes in the run-up to the Sydney Olympics.
"They are very keen to make a good showing to the world," he said.
The 14-year-old is Ian Thorpe, whose destruction of age-group records in Australia has earned him the "Thorpedo" title from the Australian media.

He is also the youngest male to ever make an Australian team, beating by one month Australian hero John Konrads, who made Australia's 1956 Olympic team at 14 years, six months. Konrads went on to win an Olympic gold medal in 1960 and set half a dozen world records.
Thorpe has swam the 400 metre freestyle in three minutes 53.44 seconds, which would had given him eighth spot in the finals at the Atlanta Olympics.
"It's pretty exciting," Thorpe's coach Doug Frost said, adding Thorpe was looking forward to the Olympics in his hometown of Sydney. "He's looking at that. That is where his goals are," Frost said.

Thorpe is just the youngest of several rising stars the Australians are developing for 2000. Frost also pointed to 16-year-old Simon Cowley, who is quickly gaining on veteran Philip Rogers, 25, as Australia's best breaststroker.
"He's an outstanding prospect as well as far as Sydney is concerned," Frost said.

Grant Hackett, a relative veteran at 17, is already ranked number one in the world in both the 800 and 1,500 freestyle and took the gold in the 1,500 at the world short-course championships in Sweden in April.

The old man of the youth brigade, by Australian standards, is Michael Klim, who turns 20 on Wednesday. Klim has been giving himself early birthday presents this week. On Sunday, he had the fastest time in the world in the last two years in winning the 200 freestyle.

His time of 1:47.60 was 0.03 second better than the gold medal time at last year's Olympics. He followed that up on Monday by swimming the 100 freestyle in 49.46, the fastest time in the world this year and an Australian and Commonwealth record.
The Australian women's team is also stocking up on youth for the Olympics, including 15-year-olds Kristy Ellem and Natasha Bowron, who both won short-course gold medals.

Bowron, who did not come to Fukuoka because she was sick, led the 800 freestyle from start to finish in Sweden. Ellem won the 200 breaststroke in 2:22.68 to become the third-fastest swimmer in the event ever.
The Pan Pacific meeting ends on Wednesday and is one of the last important events on the swimming calendar prior to next January's world championships.
